Android and the desktop carry the whole agent and have hands on their own screens; the iPhone has everything but the hands, since iOS lets no app operate another; the web app shows the same conversation from a runtime on a computer of the person’s own. The devices meet over the relay, open source and optional; the screens are drawings, not screenshots.
figures.headline: The Android phone and the desktop run the whole agent with hands on their own screens, while the iPhone has no hands.
citing_sentences: It is an argument that the open counterpart has to exist, as a complete thing a person can run. nanoMuse is our attempt at that counterpart, and Fig. 1 is the shape of it.

citing_sentences: nanoMuse is a non-profit project that would like a community; this roadmap is an offer of work in three distances, and Fig. 6 lays it out as five lanes, each Now card with a first task.

The near work is unglamorous, and the first column of Fig. 6 lists it: memory that surfaces at the right moment, proactivity between the schedules, a conversation in which a person who has used Muse does not feel the drop, hands that fail less, self-hosting in one command.

abstract: Assistants from 2011 answered and waited, and agents from 2023 did a task and stopped. In September 2026 Meta’s Muse showed an agent for one person, with accounts, devices, memory and a conversation that lasts, closed, in a vendor’s cloud, in one country. Such an agent is expected to act on a person’s accounts and devices, remember them across weeks, speak first when it is worth it, and answer for what it did. It is a kind of software, not a model, and until now had no open counterpart. This report defines the personal agent in five questions and three horizons. It reads how Muse is built from Meta’s public record and a copy of its production prompt, each statement marked by its source. It then presents nanoMuse, the open-source counterpart under the GPL-3.0, one agent on every device a person owns, with hands on the phone’s screen and the computer’s. They share one conversation over a relay anyone can run; every action goes through a Sentinel, memory is files the person can read, and the model is their choice. Its size and cost are given as estimates. What is open, memory with provenance, an evaluation suite for the hands and an open model for them, is set out as a roadmap.

sections.body: The introduction defines a personal agent as software that acts for one person on their accounts, devices and files, and argues that such an agent should be inspectable by that person and runnable on hardware they own. It describes Muse, released in September 2026 and sold in the United States only, as running in one Linux virtual machine per person in Meta's cloud, with only a small SDK open. The authors present nanoMuse as the open counterpart and list five contributions: a definition and history, a reading of Muse's construction, five questions and three horizons, nanoMuse itself, and a roadmap with limitations.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: A personal agent should be inspectable by its owner, and no open counterpart to Muse existed before this report.

sections.body: The section traces assistants such as Siri, Alexa and Google Assistant, which answered and waited, through task agents and open models that operate screens, to hosted browsers and cloud computers. Hermes Agent and OpenClaw run on a computer or server the person owns and remember across sessions, but have no screen. In September 2026 Muse, Today, OpenMuse, Manus Cue and OpenAI's dots arrived. Table 1 compares these agents with the open projects on where the agent runs, whether it operates a phone or computer screen, and its license. The authors conclude that cloud computers reach only things with an API or a web page, and that nanoMuse's hands address this gap.
sections.heading: Personal Agents So Far
sections.headline: Before September 2026, open personal agents ran on the owner's machine without screens, and screen-operating agents served single tasks.

sections.body: Based on Meta's public documents, a copy of Muse's production system prompt, and the shipped clients, this section explains how Muse is built and marks each statement as documented, prompt, observed or inferred. The authors credit its reception to its shape rather than a benchmark: one long conversation, memory as files the person can edit, and the agent's steps shown by default, among other choices. The Sentinel is the sole permission authority for connector actions and all network egress, and each person has a dedicated Linux virtual machine in Meta's cloud. The authors infer that Muse cannot operate an interface that has no accessibility tree, such as a native phone app.
sections.heading: How Muse Is Built
sections.headline: Muse's shape rests on ten visible design choices and safety layers the agent cannot reach, with a virtual machine per person.

sections.body: This section is an opinion on what a personal agent should be, answered through five questions: what it knows, where it acts, whom it answers to, how it learns, and how it is paid for and governed. For memory, the authors propose plain files with provenance and a reconciliation rule, and a line the person wrote outranks any line a model wrote. For action, one agent should serve as the person's standing representative across all their hands. For approval, grants should have scopes the person can state in a sentence, and a payment approval or a password is never remembered. Figure 4 arranges the questions as sectors across three horizons. The section states that nanoMuse, measured against these questions, falls short of most of them.
sections.heading: What a Personal Agent Should Be
sections.headline: A personal agent should answer five questions about memory, action, approval, learning and payment, across three horizons.

sections.body: nanoMuse is an open, minimal personal agent under the GPL-3.0, with an Android app, an iOS app through TestFlight, desktop apps, a web app and a relay, described at version 0.1.40. Each device runs a whole agent with its own Sentinel, which gates every tool call through a fixed decision order and records each decision in a log the person can open. On the phone, the agent operates the screen through a one-action-per-screenshot loop, and it climbs from skills and command-line tools to a browser before it reaches for the screen. Memory is Markdown files. Table 2 gives sizes: the Android app is 38 MB to download (arm64), and the relay idles at about 85 MB of memory. Cost figures are estimates from provider price lists.
sections.heading: nanoMuse Today
sections.headline: nanoMuse runs one agent on each device, operating the Android phone's screen and the computer's, with a Sentinel gating every action.

sections.body: The roadmap is an offer of work in three distances. The Now column lists the catch-up work with Muse: memory that surfaces at the right moment, proactivity, a smoother conversation, hands that fail less, and self-hosting in one command. Next comes an evaluation suite built from failed runs, run beside public suites such as AndroidWorld, OSWorld, MemGUI-Bench and OS-Harm, and a small open model for the hands trained on contributed traces. Later items, drawn dashed, include the physical world as hands, such as cameras, appliances or robot arms under the same approvals and log. The section gives no dates and asks for contributions, including small ones such as a failing trace.
sections.heading: A Roadmap With the Community
sections.headline: The open roadmap is set in three distances, from catching up with Muse to an open model for the hands and physical devices.

sections.body: The section lists four limits. On a single device the Sentinel runs in the same trust domain as the agent, so a compromise of the device is a compromise of the agent, and no host outside the agent's reach holds the real credentials as Muse does. The hands are judged by their words and by the accessibility text, and the authors have no success rate and no count of human take-overs to report. Memory does not record which model wrote a line, its date or a confidence. The community relay keeps conversation text for users who sync, and the default-on switch for improving the community's models is the choice the authors are least sure of.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: nanoMuse's Sentinel shares a trust domain with the agent, and its hands have no measured success rate.
